prompt: shop-db-1 is deleted. Its two data disks were attached with deleteOption set to Detach. What happens to shop-db-data?
hint: A disk is a resource beside the machine, with a bill of its own.

choices.text: It is deleted with the machine, because it was attached to it
choices.why: That is what Delete does. Detach leaves the disk as a resource of its own.

choices.text: It stays in Azure, attached to nothing, and is billed every hour
choices.why: Detached and intact, with the orders on it, and still on the bill until somebody deletes it.

choices.text: It is kept at no charge until another machine attaches it
choices.why: A detached disk is billed exactly as an attached one; that is how they pile up.

choices.text: It becomes a snapshot, and the disk itself is removed
choices.why: Nothing turns a disk into a snapshot by itself; a snapshot is a resource you create.

prompt: Which host caching value does Microsoft recommend for the disk that holds the database write log, and why?
hint: Think about how a log is used: written in order, read almost never.

choices.text: ReadWrite, since the log is mostly writes and that mode holds writes
choices.why: It holds them on the host and writes them later, which is safe only for software that flushes properly. For a write-heavy disk the guidance is None.

choices.text: ReadOnly, since cached reads do not count against the disk
choices.why: True of cached reads, and useless for a disk that is almost never read.

choices.text: None, since the log is written in sequence and seldom read back
choices.why: A cache helps repeated reads, and the log has none to repeat; None sends each write straight to the disk.

choices.text: ReadWrite, since that is the default of a data disk
choices.why: ReadWrite is the default of the OS disk. For data disks, two of Microsoft's pages disagree, which is why db.bicep writes the value.

prompt: A developer writes the nightly sales report to /dev/disk/azure/resource on a Standard_D4ds_v5, because it is fast. Which of these is documented as able to lose it?
hint: That path is the temporary disk, on the host.

choices.text: A restart from inside the operating system
choices.why: Microsoft documents that data on the temporary disk persists through a successful standard restart.

choices.text: A snapshot taken of the OS disk
choices.why: A snapshot reads a managed disk; it does not touch the temporary disk at all.

choices.text: The machine being stopped and deallocated
choices.why: Stopping, a redeploy or a maintenance event can lose it, because the disk belongs to the host and not to the machine.

choices.text: Turning on ReadOnly caching for the data disk
choices.why: That reattaches the data disk it is set on. The temporary disk is not a managed disk and has no caching setting.

prompt: In db.bicep the data disk and the log disk are told apart by a logical unit number, written as ___: 0 and 1.
hint: The three letters stand for logical unit number.

prompt: Put in order the steps of moving shop-db-data to another machine.
hint: Inside the machine first, then Azure.
items: Stop the database writing to the disk
Unmount the file system and remove its line from /etc/fstab
Detach the disk with az vm disk detach
Attach it to a machine in the same zone
trap: Detaching a disk that is still mounted pulls it from under a running file system.

prompt: A Standard_D2ds_v5 (3,750 IOPS uncached, its burst credits spent) has two P30 data disks of 5,000 IOPS each, caching None. A job asks both disks for everything they have. How many IOPS does it get in total?
hint: The lower of what the disks offer together and what the machine allows.

prompt: What is the most IOPS a 40 GiB Premium SSD v2 disk may be given?
hint: Above 6 GiB, 500 per GiB, up to 80,000.

prompt: Which of these are true of Premium SSD v2? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three numbers, and three limits that come with them.

choices.text: It cannot be used as an OS disk
choices.why: It is a data disk only, like Ultra Disk.

choices.text: It is sold in P tiers, like Premium SSD
choices.why: It has no tiers: any size in steps of 1 GiB, with IOPS and MB/s set apart.

choices.text: Its attachment takes no host caching
choices.why: Microsoft lists host caching among what it does not support; the attachment says None.

choices.text: It can be zone-redundant, as PremiumV2_ZRS
choices.why: ZRS is offered for Premium SSD and Standard SSD, not for v2; the CLI lists no such SKU.

choices.text: Its first 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s carry no charge
choices.why: That baseline comes with every disk; only what is set above it is billed.

prompt: A 1 TiB Premium SSD (P30) runs above its 5,000 IOPS for several hours every working day. What does Microsoft's guidance point to?
hint: Bursting is for short spells; which model fits a P30 at all?

choices.text: Credit-based bursting, which costs nothing extra
choices.why: Credit-based bursting covers Premium SSDs of 512 GiB and less, and a full bucket lasts 30 minutes.

choices.text: A higher performance tier, at a fixed price
choices.why: A disk that would otherwise run in burst most of the time belongs in a higher tier, at a fixed price per tier.

choices.text: On-demand bursting left on, since it has no fixed fee
choices.why: It has an hourly fee while enabled plus every operation above the tier, and Microsoft calls it uneconomic for frequent bursts.

choices.text: ReadWrite caching, so the writes stop counting against the disk
choices.why: Cached writes still reach the disk when the cache is flushed, and count then.

prompt: disk-small.bicep, an 8 GiB Premium SSD v2 with 5,000 IOPS, compiled with no warning. Why?
hint: What does the compiler check: each value, or the relation between two?

choices.text: 8 GiB allows 5,000 IOPS, so there was nothing to catch
choices.why: From 6 GiB the limit is 500 per GiB, so 8 GiB allows 4,000. Azure would refuse it.

choices.text: Bicep skips the checks on Premium SSD v2 disks
choices.why: It checked the same disk a moment earlier and refused the throughput written as text.

choices.text: The limit linking the two is Azure's rule
choices.why: Both numbers are valid integers. The arithmetic linking IOPS to size is checked by Azure when the request arrives.

choices.text: The warning is printed only when the template is deployed
choices.why: The compiler prints its warnings on build; it printed one for the text throughput.

prompt: A staging web server with an ephemeral OS disk is not needed overnight. How do you stop paying for its compute until the morning?
hint: One of the usual ways is in the table of what you give up.

choices.text: Stop and deallocate it, as with any machine
choices.why: Stop-deallocate is not supported with an ephemeral OS disk.

choices.text: Snapshot its OS disk, then deallocate it
choices.why: An ephemeral OS disk cannot be snapshotted, and the machine cannot be deallocated either.

choices.text: Detach the OS disk and keep the machine
choices.why: An OS disk is not detached from a running machine, and an ephemeral one is not a managed disk to keep.

choices.text: Delete it, and create it again in the morning
choices.why: That is what Microsoft says to do instead, and for a machine that keeps nothing it loses nothing.

prompt: A Standard_D2ds_v5 has a 75 GiB temporary disk. An ephemeral OS disk from a 30 GiB image is placed on it, without Trusted Launch. How many GiB of temporary disk are left?
hint: The temporary disk shrinks by the size of the image.

prompt: Match each event to what it does to an ephemeral OS disk.
hint: Which events move the machine to another host, and which one is refused outright?

pairs.right: Deleted, and the OS provisioned again

right_distractors: Kept, and billed as a managed disk

prompt: Which of these machines is a poor fit for an ephemeral OS disk?
hint: Look for the one that relies on something the table says is not supported.

choices.text: A web server in a scale set whose image carries all it runs
choices.why: The case the feature is designed for: nothing on its OS disk is worth keeping, and reimage is the repair.

choices.text: A jump host stopped and deallocated every night
choices.why: Stop-deallocate is not supported, so the nightly saving it was built around is impossible.

choices.text: A build agent that is reimaged after every job
choices.why: A fast reimage to the original state is exactly what an ephemeral OS disk gives.

choices.text: A Spot machine that is deleted when it is evicted
choices.why: Ephemeral OS disks are supported on Spot machines, deleted rather than deallocated.

prompt: web-wrong.bicep, with caching ReadWrite and placement TempDisk on an ephemeral OS disk, compiled with no warning. What does that tell you?
hint: Recall what the compiler did refuse in the first section.

choices.text: TempDisk is accepted as another name for ResourceDisk
choices.why: The CLI lists CacheDisk, NvmeDisk and ResourceDisk; TempDisk is a name from the prose, not a value.

choices.text: Bicep turns ReadWrite into ReadOnly for an ephemeral disk
choices.why: The template carried ReadWrite exactly as written; the compiler changes no values.

choices.text: Both values fit the types; the rules are Azure's
choices.why: The placement is checked only as a string and ReadWrite is a known caching value; the rule linking them to an ephemeral disk is the service's.

choices.text: Both are correct, and only full caching needs ReadOnly
choices.why: Microsoft's deployment guide sets ReadOnly for every ephemeral OS disk, partial or full.

prompt: Why not attach one managed disk to all the shop's web servers for the uploaded photos?
hint: Azure allows a shared disk. What does it need on top?

choices.text: A managed disk may only ever be attached to a single machine
choices.why: Shared disks exist; Microsoft documents attaching one disk to several machines for clusters.

choices.text: Only a ZRS disk may be attached to more than one machine
choices.why: Sharing is not a ZRS feature; ZRS only adds attaching from machines in other zones.

choices.text: Sharing needs a cluster manager to decide who writes
choices.why: Pacemaker or Windows Server Failover Clustering handles the locking; Azure Files does the sharing for you.

choices.text: Disks hold blocks, and photos are files that need an object store
choices.why: A file system on a disk holds photos perfectly well; the problem is several machines writing it.

prompt: What IOPS does Microsoft recommend for a 1,024 GiB SSD share on provisioned v2?
hint: 3,000 plus one per GiB.

prompt: An NFS share in Azure Files needs the ___ media tier, which the CLI calls premium.
hint: Two media tiers: one solid-state, one spinning.

prompt: files.bicep switches public network access off and declares no private endpoint. Deployed as it stands, who can mount the uploads share?
hint: NFS has no user sign-in; what is it authenticated by?

choices.text: Any machine in brazilsouth with the aznfs helper installed
choices.why: The helper encrypts the traffic; it does not give a route to an account with no endpoint.

choices.text: Any client that holds the storage account key
choices.why: NFS shares do not take the key; they rely on the network rules alone.

choices.text: Any virtual network in the same subscription
choices.why: Reaching a share takes a private endpoint, or a service endpoint the rules allow; being in the subscription is neither.

choices.text: Nobody: the account has no reachable address
choices.why: The public endpoint is off and nothing else was declared, so there is no address to mount.

prompt: Why is the Azure Files section read rather than practised, when the lab has Azurite?
hint: Look at the three ports Azurite's help lists.

choices.text: Azurite serves blob, queue and table storage, and no file service
choices.why: Its help lists three ports, 10000 to 10002, and none of them is for files.

choices.text: Azurite has a file service, but it needs an Azure account to start
choices.why: Azurite needs no account at all; it has no file service to start.

choices.text: NFS cannot be mounted from inside a Docker container
choices.why: Not the reason given: there is nothing on the laptop to mount in the first place.

choices.text: Azure Files is not offered in the brazilsouth region
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the reason is what the emulator serves.

prompt: Match each piece of the shop's data to where this lesson puts it.
hint: Ask of each: is it shared, is it kept, and how is it used?

pairs.right: A Premium SSD v2 data disk

pairs.left: The OS of a web server in a scale set

right_distractors: A snapshot of the OS disk

prompt: To save money, shop-db-1 moves from a Standard_D4ds_v5 to a Standard_D2ds_v5. Its Premium SSD v2 data disk stays at 5,000 IOPS and 145 MB/s. Once the machine's burst credits are spent, what can its disks deliver, uncached?
hint: The D2ds_v5 row of the Ddsv5 table.

choices.text: 5,000 IOPS and 145 MB/s, because the disk is provisioned for them
choices.why: The disk can do that; the machine takes less, and the program gets the lower of the two.

choices.text: 3,750 IOPS and 145 MB/s, because a size only caps IOPS
choices.why: A size caps throughput too: 85 MB/s on the D2ds_v5.

choices.text: At most 3,750 IOPS and 85 MB/s, for all its disks together
choices.why: Those are the size's uncached limits, shared by the data disk, the log and the OS disk.

choices.text: Nothing changes until the disk is resized to match the machine
choices.why: The cap applies at once; nothing about the disk has to change for it.

prompt: A read on a data disk with ReadOnly caching misses the host cache. Put what happens in order.
hint: The disk answers the cache and the machine at once.
items: The host cache does not hold the block
The read goes over the network to the managed disk
The disk returns the block to the cache and to the machine
trap: A miss counts against both the cached and the uncached limits, because it passes through both.

prompt: Which of these mistakes did the Bicep compiler refuse in this lesson?
hint: It refused a wrong type, and a value outside a list it knows.

choices.text: The disk SKU written Premium_V2_LRS
choices.why: The SKU name is a plain string to the compiler; it went into the template.

choices.text: The data disk in zone 2 and the machine in zone 1
choices.why: Each zone is a valid string; the mismatch is Azure's to refuse.

choices.text: The share protocol written NFSv4
choices.why: enabledProtocols is a string to the compiler; NFSv4 reached the template.

choices.text: The caching value written none, in lower case
choices.why: Caching is typed as None, ReadOnly or ReadWrite, so none was refused with BCP036.
